rv.q: The five-character family drama feels even more powerful -- a boldly conventional yet altogether gripping work that knows individual psychology as keenly as it understands the world around it.
Jon Robin Baitz has written a play that is both deeply personal and utterly theatrical.

Jon Robin Baitz has written a family drama that crackles with the electricity of old wounds being picked at until they bleed afresh. This is a smart, savage and ultimately moving portrait of a family whose love for one another is both their salvation and their curse.
The script crackles with life and so do the performances.
He just makes spending time with these messed-up, complicated people a genuine pleasure.

With humor, sensitivity and invigorating anger, Baitz is doing here what he set out to do in Brothers & Sisters as originally conceived, which is to examine the fractiousness of American politics through the prism of one family.
Jon Robin Baitz has written a smart, sophisticated family drama that crackles with wit and bristles with political tension.
Baitz has crafted an assortment of people who repeatedly defy any urge to pigeonhole or judge them.
The show's second-act fireworks seem like a fittingly all-American way to celebrate the arrival of a major new play.
Together, the five performers comprise what is no doubt the finest ensemble cast currently treading the boards in New York.

Under Mantello's directional finesse, this exceptional five-member cast turns Baitz's blueprint of family squabbling into a portrait of regret and denial that is as witty and entertaining as it is emotionally cathartic.
They've even done some subtle tinkering that makes the proceedings even more effective, if that's possible.
The one thing that comes across with great power in both productions of this play for grown-ups is the sense of a dilemma that few of us can escape
Even as skilled a director (and frequent Baitz collaborator) as Joe Mantello can't keep the thing from sinking in implausibility.

cn.t: Baitz's smart family drama about a fraught holiday reunion crackles with wit and strong performances, particularly Rachel Griffiths' Broadway debut, though some critics find the escalating revelations strain credibility.

sg.ra: The Booth is one of Broadway's smallest houses at 766 seats, so center orchestra rows C-H give close-up detail of plays and intimate dramas without paying the very-front premium. Row AA front offers max legroom (Headout) but stage is high; step back a few rows for better sightline onto the stage floor.

sg.vl: Workable angle, not the sweet spot
sg.ra: Booth is narrow so side orchestra remains viable, but a 2018 BWW forum post specifically flagged 'angle from the front side seats' as a concern. Closer rows (BB, A) on the side get awkward angles onto the high stage. Mid-house aisle seats recover the view while adding legroom.
sg.rr: A-P (17 rows, odd 1-15 left, even 2-16 right)

sg.ra: In a 252-seat mezzanine with only 8 rows, even the back row is close. SeatPlan and Headout both call Center Mezz A-B some of the best seats in the house, and G-H are cited as strong value. With the Booth's intimate scale, the mezzanine never feels distant — this is the value pick.

sg.vl: Small house saves the side angle
sg.ra: SeatPlan explicitly notes side-mezz views are 'slightly more angled but still viable' because the Booth is narrow. Decent budget alternative, but the center mezz is a better value at similar price tier so this is solid-not-sweet.
